kurz: Unlike the return, costs are fixed by contract, and they are charged on the entire invested assets even in years with losses.

bloecke.md: Of everything that happens in a portfolio, only the costs are known in advance. The return is an expectation; the costs are agreed by contract. A fund with ongoing charges of 1.5% deducts this 1.5% even in a year in which the market loses a third, because the charges are calculated on the fund assets and not on the return. Every tenth of a percentage point saved therefore improves the result in the portfolio with certainty, whereas an additional idea for boosting returns does so only with a certain probability.

## Costs in relation to return

In the usual presentation, fees look small because they appear next to double-digit price movements. The meaningful comparison, however, is with the expected return. With a gross return of 7%, costs of 1.5 percentage points amount to around 21% of the return. In a money market or bond fund with a gross return of 3%, the same 1.5 percentage points correspond to half of the return. A single percentage point, which the examples in this lesson use, is around a seventh of the return at 7% gross and a third at 3%.

This gives a rule of thumb that does not come up in sales conversations. The lower the expected return of an asset class, the lower its costs should be. An expensive bond fund is therefore even harder to justify mathematically than an expensive equity fund.

The **basis of calculation** for almost all fees is the assets, not the profit. That is why fees are charged in full even in years with losses. In addition, they grow with the portfolio without the service in return increasing.

bloecke.md:
## Types of cost and bases of calculation

The costs of an investment consist of half a dozen items that are charged in different places. More important than whether they are high or low is the distinction between ongoing and one-off costs. Ongoing costs have the same effect every year. One-off costs are spread over the holding period, and their effect per year becomes smaller the longer you hold the investment.

bloecke.md:
## TER and tracking difference

The total expense ratio ([[TER]]) includes the costs of management, the custodian bank, auditing and the index licence fees. It does not include the transaction costs that the fund itself pays when trading, or the performance fee. A fund with high portfolio turnover is therefore more expensive than its TER suggests.

For index funds, the [[tracking difference]] is more meaningful. It measures how far the fund's return lags behind the index return over several years and captures costs, withholding tax treatment, sampling deviations and income from securities lending together. Since 2010, the iShares Core MSCI World has had a TER of 0.20% but an average shortfall of around 0.03 percentage points. The fund therefore earns back a large part of its fee through securities lending and its tax structure. This is not guaranteed for the future, because both sources of income can disappear, and the figures for individual years vary considerably. When comparing index funds, you should therefore look at the tracking difference over several years rather than at the decimal places of the TER.

## Converting one-off costs

An initial charge of 5% is added on top of the net amount invested. Of a €1,000 payment, €952.38 therefore goes into the fund, so the fee amounts to 4.76% of the amount paid in. More meaningful than this percentage is converting it to the holding period. With a holding period of five years, the same 5% reduces the return by around 0.97 percentage points a year; with twenty years, by only 0.24. Investors who switch every three years pay the charge again every three years.

bloecke.erklaerung: The formula converts a one-off purchase fee into an annual drag on the return.
variablen: Initial charge as a decimal, for example 0.05 for 5%
bloecke.beispiel: With a = 0.05 and n = 20, the result is 1 - (1/1.05)^(1/20) = 0.0024, that is, 0.24 percentage points a year. With n = 5 it is 0.97 percentage points, with n = 30 only 0.16.

bloecke.md:
## One percentage point of costs over thirty years

€10,000 is invested for thirty years at a gross return of 7%. Without costs, the amount grows to €76,123; with one percentage point of ongoing charges, to €57,435. The gap of €18,688 is just under a quarter of the final wealth and results from a figure that looks like a minor detail in the prospectus.

Of this gap, around €7,900 is fees paid over the thirty years. The remaining €10,800 or so is the return that these fees would have earned in the portfolio. A fee therefore costs its own amount plus all the returns that this amount would have produced by the end of the investment period. This is why the share lost in the chart above grows with the investment period, and why, for long-term savings plans, the cost ratio has greater financial consequences than any other decision.

A savings plan of €300 a month runs for thirty years, with €108,000 paid in.

- At 7% net, the result is around €366,000.
- At 6% net, it is around €301,400.

The difference of around €64,600 is more than half of the amount paid in and results from a difference of one percentage point a year. (Illustrative calculation with a constant return and monthly compounding, before tax.)

bloecke.md:
## Active funds and the market return

In 1991 William Sharpe showed that this relationship is not an empirical question. All investors together hold the market. The average actively managed euro must therefore earn exactly the market return before costs and necessarily less after costs. The result follows from the arithmetic itself, and no study can refute it. John Bogle derived the *Cost Matters Hypothesis* from this. According to this hypothesis, it does not matter whether markets are efficient, because the net return always equals the gross return minus costs.

The European figures are consistent with this. According to ESMA's cost data for the ten-year period to 2021, active equity funds in the EU cost 1.50% a year, passive funds 0.53% and ETFs 0.31%. Net returns were 9.4% compared with 10.6% and 10.4% a year. The gap roughly corresponds to the difference in costs. The shortfall of active funds is therefore explained by their costs and need not be attributed to poor security selection.

bloecke.md:
Percentage-based execution fees rise with the monthly contribution. A fee of 1.75% looks small, but with a €300 contribution it comes to €63 a year. With a portfolio value of a few thousand euros, that is more than the entire fund fee. Compared with a flat fee of €1.50, the percentage fee is only cheaper for contributions below around €86.

The label “free” is a sales term. The provider finances zero-fee executions through other income. Inducements from trading venues, which used to pay for them, have been banned in Germany too since 1 July 2026 (Article 39a MiFIR). Promotional lists of fee-free ETFs can end at any time. The costs of a zero-fee purchase are contained in the spread rather than in the contract note.

1. Check the ongoing charges in the key information document before buying, not in the advertising material.
2. For index funds, compare the tracking difference over several years instead of just the TER.
3. Convert one-off costs to the planned holding period, because only then are they comparable with ongoing costs.
4. Always trade with a limit order and buy or sell world ETFs between 15:30 and 17:30, because the US stock exchanges are open then and spreads are at their narrowest.
5. Reallocations are a double burden. They cost the spread and the order fee and also end the tax deferral.

The key information document (PRIIPs KID) shows the costs in two forms: as a reduction in yield per year for different holding periods, and as a breakdown into entry, exit and ongoing costs, transaction costs and performance fees. The reduction in yield for the shortest holding period is the most meaningful figure in the document, because it includes the one-off costs.

The fund's annual report states the portfolio turnover, the securities lending and how the lending income is split. At iShares, 62.5% of the lending income goes to the fund and the provider keeps 37.5%.

The bank's schedule of prices and services lists the custody fee, order fees, trading venue fees and third-party charges. The terms change frequently, so every figure should come with a date.

The reduction in yield stated for insurance policies is the only figure that includes the costs of the entire wrapper. The TER of the fund inside says nothing about the policy on its own.

mitnehmen: Costs are charged on assets, not on profits, so they are incurred in full even in years with losses.

begriffe.text: Total expense ratio of a fund. It covers the ongoing costs of management, custodian bank, auditing and index licence, which are deducted pro rata from the fund assets every day. The fund's transaction costs and performance fees are not included.

Measured shortfall of the fund return compared with the index return over a period. The figure captures costs, withholding tax, sampling and income from securities lending together and is therefore more meaningful than the TER.
One-off sales charge when buying fund units, added on top of the net amount invested. A 5% charge corresponds to 4.76% of the amount paid in.

Legally required figure for insurance products (VVG-Informationspflichtenverordnung, Insurance Information Obligations Ordinance). It states the annual reduction in return caused by all the costs of the contract, including the acquisition and administration costs of the wrapper.
Highest unit value that a fund must exceed before a performance fee is charged again. This prevents a fee from being charged merely for making up a loss.
